The remedy is general because it's complete: every type of song, every state of the soul, covered. Whatever the fall, one of the ten reaches it. Whatever the song, one of the ten sings it.
296.practice: Count your ten — the ten parts of your life needing remedy (or ten gratitudes, if the day is kind): health, family, work, heart... One line each. The ten, surveyed — the remedy knows where to go.

297.title: The Psalms of the Depths
body: Some of the ten go down: Psalm 42 ("as the hart pants after the water"), Psalm 77 (the night of trouble), Psalm 137 (by the rivers of Babylon, we wept).
The remedy doesn't skip the depths — it includes them. Healing isn't the denial of the fall; it's the psalm from the fall. The general remedy covers the low places because it visits them.
Whatever depth you're in: there's a psalm already there.
297.practice: If you're low, read Psalm 42 today — slowly, as your own words. If you're not, read it for someone who is. The depths, psalmed.

298.title: The Psalms of the Heights
body: And some of the ten go up: Psalm 150 (every breath, praise!), Psalm 105 (give thanks), Psalm 16 (the pleasant portion).

The remedy includes the heights too — because healing isn't only repair, it's ascent. The general remedy doesn't just fix the broken; it lifts the whole. Praise is medicine: the soul, singing, is the soul healing (the year's refrain).
298.practice: Read Psalm 150 today — all six verses, out loud if you can. Let every breath praise ("kol haneshamah tehallel"). The heights, psalmed. The remedy, sung.

299.title: Tinyana 92
body: The Likutei Moharan year ends on 6 Tishrei with Tinyana 92 — the lesson of the Tikkun HaKlali.

The last lesson is the remedy: after 364 days of Torahs — light, faith, joy, prayer, the tzadik within — the curriculum closes with healing. Not with a final exam. With a remedy. The tradition knows its students: they'll need it.
Begin with light (Lesson 1); end with healing (Tinyana 92). The year's arc, complete.

(The remedy surfaces once before the end: Torah 205, on Erev Pesach, introduces the Tikkun — revealed at the Exodus, completed before Yom Kippur. From leaving Egypt to the day of atonement: the whole arc, healed.)
299.practice: Read all ten psalms today — or begin with three (the rule): 16, 150, and one from the depths (42 or 77). The year's last lesson, lived on any day: the remedy, taken.
299.teaser: the remedy, lived: how to take it.

300.title: Taking the Remedy
body: How do you "take" ten psalms? The tradition's way:

Say them — in order, with intention. Not rushed: the remedy works by coverage, and coverage takes time. Some say them for a specific fall; some, as maintenance — the soul's daily vitamin. Rebbe Nachman promised: the general remedy covers the general condition.
And the deeper taking: live them. The psalm of the depths, lived in the depths. The psalm of praise, lived in praise. The ten, not just said — inhabited.
300.practice: Take the remedy today: the ten psalms (or your three), said slowly, in order, with intention. Then one lived: carry a verse into the day. The remedy, taken.
300.teaser: the week closes: healed, and singing.

301.title: Healed, and Singing
body: The week closes: the General Remedy — ten psalms, the depths and the heights, the year's last lesson.

The curriculum's promise: the falls are real, and the remedy is general. Nothing is beyond the ten — not the depth (there's a psalm there), not the height (there's a psalm there too). The soul, whatever its condition, has its medicine.
And the medicine is song. The remedy isn't a pill; it's psalms. Healing, in this tradition, sings.
301.practice: Sing one psalm today — any of the ten, any tune, any voice. The remedy's last instruction: the healed soul sings. So sing.
301.teaser: David, the general soul: Adam, David, Mashiach.

302.title: The General Soul
body: Neshamah Klali: the general soul — the soul that contains all souls. King David, the tradition says, was one: his psalms hold everyone's emotions. Whatever you feel, David felt it first — and sang it.
That's why the Book of Psalms is "the general prayer book": not one man's songs, but every person's. The general soul sings generally — and each particular soul finds its verse.
302.practice: Find your verse today: open the Psalms (anywhere), read until one line stops you. That's David, singing your emotion. The general soul, particularized — for you.

303.title: Adam, David, Mashiach
body: One soul, three lives: Adam, David, Mashiach.

Adam: the first man — the soul, given. David: the sweet singer — the soul, singing. Mashiach: the redeemer — the soul, completed. The tradition reads them as one arc: the soul's giving, its song, its redemption.
And the letters spell it: Adam — David — Mashiach. The soul's story, in initials.
303.practice: Place yourself on the arc: given (what were you given?), singing (what's your song?), completed (what's still coming?). One line each. The soul's story, in your initials.

304.title: The Sweet Singer
body: David: the shepherd who became king, the warrior who sang. The tradition's image: harp at the head of the bed, waking at midnight to sing (the Chatzot hours — the year's own midnight practice).

The sweet singer's secret: he sang everything — the triumphs and the sins, the heights (Psalm 150) and the depths (Psalm 51, after the fall). No censoring. The general soul's generality: every emotion, admitted and sung.
304.practice: Sing the unsung today — the emotion you censor (the anger, the grief, the embarrassing joy): give it one verse, one tune, one honest minute. David's secret: everything, sung.

305.title: Psalm 89:33
body: The book's summary verse: "VeChasdi lo afir me'imo" — "My kindness I will not remove from him" (Psalm 89:33).

As "the righteous shall live by his faith" summarizes the Torah, this summarizes the Psalms: the whole 150 songs, in one promise — My kindness will not be removed. Whatever the psalm (depth or height, sin or praise), the frame holds: the kindness, unremoved.
Carry it as the week's verse: the Psalms' bottom line.
305.practice: Say it today — in Hebrew or English: "My kindness I will not remove." (Or hear it said to you: His kindness, unremoved, from you.) The summary verse, carried.

306.title: Everyone's Emotions
body: 150 psalms: the tradition says they contain every human emotion. Grief (137), guilt (51), terror (91), ecstasy (150), doubt (73), trust (23), rage (109), tenderness (131)...
Whatever you feel has a psalm. That's the general prayer book's promise: you're never the first to feel it, and never alone in it. David felt it, sang it, and left the song.
The soul's curriculum, in 150 songs: the emotional education, complete.
306.practice: Name today's emotion — precisely (not "bad": which bad?). Then find its psalm (ask, search, or guess — the finding is the practice). The emotion, psalmed. The education, continued.

307.title: The Midnight Harp
body: David's harp, at the head of the bed: the midnight wind would play it, waking him to sing. The tradition's image of the general soul: woken by the night, singing.

The year's midnight practice (the Mochin hours, the 15 ma'alot) is David's harp, institutionalized: the night, playing; the soul, waking; the song, sung. Chatzot — midnight — the seam where the year turns (week 1's teaching): David's hour.
307.practice: Wake once in the night — or honor the waking: if you stir at midnight, don't just roll over. One verse, one breath of song. The harp, played. David's hour, kept.
307.teaser: the week closes: the general soul, and yours.

308.title: The General Soul, and Yours
body: The week closes: David — the general soul, the sweet singer, Adam-to-Mashiach, the 150 emotions, the midnight harp, the unremoved kindness.

And yours: the particular soul, with its particular verse. The general contains the particular — that's what "general soul" means. Your verse is in there. Your emotion's been sung. Your midnight has its harp.
The curriculum's penultimate teaching: you're not alone in the song. You never were.
308.practice: Sing your verse today — the one you found on Day 302 (or a new one). Aloud, if you can. The general soul's gift to the particular: your song was already sung. Now sing it.
308.teaser: the soul needs to sing: the movement closes, the curriculum gathers.

309.title: The Song of the Soul
body: "This blog's objective is to bring us closer to our song — the song of the soul."

The soul has a song: not a metaphor — the tradition means it nearly literally. Each soul, its melody; each life, its lyrics. The curriculum's whole work (the levels, the lessons, the remedy) is to bring you closer to yours.

"The reality is that our soul needs to sing! Yet what are we to do if we do not know the melody and the lyrics of the song?" The year's answer: the calendar is the sheet music. Learn the music; find the song.
309.practice: Hum today — deliberately, even tunelessly. Not a song you know: yours, whatever comes. The soul's song, warming up.

310.title: The Curriculum, Gathered
body: Seven weeks, one line each:

The levels: five depths, one soul (week 39). The year: a lesson a day, 25 Elul→6 Tishrei (week 40). The co-author: the calendar writes half the lines (week 41). The tzadik: the righteous one, within (week 42). The remedy: ten psalms, the depths and heights (week 43). The general soul: David — your verse is in there (week 44). The song: the soul needs to sing (week 45).
The soul's curriculum: know your depths, learn your lessons, hear your co-author, meet your tzadik, take your remedy, find your verse — and sing.
310.practice: Read the seven lines aloud. Which one pulls? That's your next study — the curriculum, personalized. Follow the pull.

311.title: The Melody and the Lyrics
body: The melody: the year's — the cycles, the seasons, the sheet music. Given. You don't compose the melody; you learn it. The 52 weeks, the ten cycles, the microcosms: the melody, taught.
The lyrics: yours — the life, the falls, the remedy, the verse. Not given; lived. The five levels, the tzadik within, the psalm you found: the lyrics, written daily.
The song needs both: melody without lyrics is humming; lyrics without melody is talking. Together: the song of the soul.
311.practice: One melody-line (a cycle's teaching, carried) + one lyric-line (your day's truth, written): put them together. The song, in two lines.

312.title: Singing, as Practice
body: Singing isn't the curriculum's decoration. It's the practice.

The animals sing (Perek Shirah). David sang (the Psalms). Hannah sang (the answered prayer). The remedy is songs. Joy is commanded — and joy sings. The soul that sings is the soul that's healing, returning, completing.
You don't need a voice. You need the willingness: the hum, the verse aloud, the psalm murmured. The tradition doesn't grade the singing. It counts the singers.
312.practice: Sing once today — really: a psalm, a verse, a niggun, a hum-with-intent. The practice, practiced. The soul, singing.

313.title: The Sheet Music, Revisited
body: "The Jewish calendar itself is its sheet music."

Revisit it now, with the curriculum behind you: the calendar doesn't just schedule the song — it scores it. The festivals (the movements), the fasts (the minor keys), the Sabbaths (the rests), the new moons (the reprises). The year, as composition.
And you're the musician: the levels are your instrument (five strings), the lessons your technique, the remedy your tuning, David your teacher. The sheet music was always there. Now you can read it.
313.practice: Read one week as music: the coming seven days — movements, keys, rests, reprises. Score it, lightly. Then play it.
313.teaser: the movement closes: the examined song.

314.title: The Examined Song
body: The unexamined song isn't worth singing? No — the tradition is kinder: the unheard song is worth finding.

Examine yours: the melody (what have you learned this year?), the lyrics (what have you lived?), the voice (which level sings loudest? which is silent?). The curriculum's final exam isn't a test — it's a listening. Hear your song. Then sing it truer.
314.practice: Listen to your year: three melodies learned, three lyrics lived, one silent string (the level to wake). Written down. The song, examined — and ready.
314.teaser: the curriculum, kept: how to keep singing.

315.title: Keeping the Song
body: How do you keep it — the song, the curriculum, the singing?

The year's way: the levels, visited (the two-minute sit). The lesson, daily (read, carry, tie, review). The co-author, heard (ask the date). The tzadik, visited. The remedy, taken (the ten, or your three). The verse, sung. The melody, learned; the lyrics, lived.
Begin with three (the rule outlasts the movement): three of these, kept daily. The smallest becomes a thousand.
The soul needs to sing. Now it knows how.
315.practice: Pick your three. Write them. Begin today. The curriculum, kept. The song, sung.
315.teaser: Movement VII: Living It. The journal, the review, making the practice permanent.

316.title: The Witness
body: Forty-six weeks. You've walked the day, sung the songs (almost — they're coming), spelled the alphabet, turned the ten cycles, entered the worlds inside times, and studied the soul's curriculum.
Now: write it down. Not the curriculum — your year. The journal is the witness: the one who was there, who saw what happened, who remembers what the weeks did to you.

Memory lies. Not maliciously — it just edits. The week that bored you in March becomes, by September, the week that changed everything, or the week that never happened. The journal doesn't edit. It testifies.
316.practice: Get a notebook — paper, not an app. Paper remembers differently. Write today's date and one sentence: where you are, forty-six weeks in.
316.teaser: what to write, and what to leave out.

317.title: The One Line
body: The journal's enemy is ambition. "I'll write everything" becomes "I'll write nothing" by Thursday.

So: one line. Each day, one line — the day's face, in your words. Not the curriculum's words; yours. "The week of Hod: I finally heard the silence." "Tiferet: the argument with my brother, and the beauty after."
One line is enough because one line is true. Ten pages of summary is the curriculum repeating itself; one line is you, answering back.
317.practice: Write one line about this week so far. Just one. Make it yours, not the book's.
317.teaser: the weekly entry: the portrait, in your hand.

318.title: The Weekly Portrait
body: Once a week — Shabbat, when the week is complete — write the portrait. The week's face, as you saw it. Three prompts, if you need them: What lit up? What resisted? What stays?

This is the week's summary, but translated — out of the curriculum's language and into your life. "The week of Netzach: the forty days. I didn't climb a mountain; I kept showing up to the same difficult conversation." That's the portrait. The curriculum gave the frame; you supply the picture.
318.practice: Write this week's portrait — three sentences, one per prompt. Lit up, resisted, stays.
318.teaser: the honest page: what didn't work.

319.title: The Honest Page
body: Some weeks bounced off. Some practices you skipped. Some days the whole thing felt like someone else's religion.

Write that down too. The honest page is the journal's most valuable page — because the curriculum only works on the life you actually have, not the life you perform. "Week 33: I didn't feel the linchpin. I felt tired." That's data. That's the truth the next year will build on.
The tradition has no use for fake piety. The journal has no use for it either.
319.practice: Write one honest sentence about a week that didn't land. No justification, no guilt. Just the truth.
319.teaser: rereading: the journal as a mirror.

320.title: The Mirror
body: Every few weeks, reread. Not to grade — to see. The journal is a mirror with a delay: you read what you wrote a month ago and meet someone slightly different from who you are now.

That's the point. The curriculum is slow; the changes are slow; without the mirror you'd miss them. "I wrote 'I can't sit still' in week 12. In week 40 I wrote 'the silence held me.'" Nobody told you you'd changed. The mirror did.
320.practice: Reread your first entries — or, if you're just starting the journal now, write the first entry as a letter to the you who'll reread it in a month.
320.teaser: the marked days: holidays, falls, remedies.

321.title: The Marked Days
body: Mark the days that marked you. The holiday that landed differently this year. The fall — and the remedy you took. The week the linchpin clicked. The day the song finally sang.

A journal with marked days becomes a map: here be dragons, here be water. Next year, when you walk the cycle again, you'll know where the ground is soft and where it's solid. The curriculum repeats; your map makes the repetition a return, not a rerun.
321.practice: Go back through your entries and mark three days — star them, date them, name them. Your year's holy days.

322.title: The Offering
body: At the end: the journal is an offering. Not to the curriculum — to the One the curriculum serves. Your year, bound. Your witness, given.

There's an old image: the Book of Life, written on Rosh Hashanah. Your journal is the rough draft — the life, as lived, in your hand, before it's sealed. Writing it is a kind of prayer: this is what I did with the year You gave me.
Forty-six weeks. The witness has testified. Now: look back over it all.
322.practice: Close the notebook. Hold it a moment. Then open it to the first page and read the first line you wrote. That's where you started.
322.teaser: the review: forty-nine weeks in one sitting.

323.title: The Sitting
body: This week: the review. One sitting — an hour, maybe two — with the journal, the year spread out before you.

Start at the beginning. Week 1: the day. Read your lines. Then walk forward — the songs, the letters, the cycles, the worlds, the soul — week by week, in order. Don't rush. The year took a year; give the review an hour.
You're not studying. You're remembering — which is a different act. Studying asks "what does it mean?" Remembering asks "what happened to me?"
323.practice: Schedule the sitting — today or Shabbat. An hour, the journal, no phone. The year, spread out.
323.teaser: the before and after: what changed.

324.title: The Before and After
body: As you review, hold two pictures: the you who started, and the you who's sitting here.
What changed? Not "what did you learn" — what changed. The practice you actually do now. The reaction you don't have anymore. The morning that feels different. The blessing you say and mean.
Some changes are small and they're the real ones. "I notice the light at 2 PM now" is worth more than "I understand the sefirot." The curriculum aimed at the life, not the library.
324.practice: Write two sentences. "Before this year, I ___." "Now, I ___." The before and after, in your hand.

325.title: The Weeks That Sang
body: Some weeks lit up. You'll know them in the review — the entries get longer, the lines get truer, the practices actually happened.

Name them. Three, maybe five. These are your weeks — the ones where the curriculum met your life and something caught fire. They tell you something about your soul: what it's hungry for, what language it speaks, where it's going.
Next year, linger on these weeks. Give them more time. The curriculum is the same for everyone; the lingering is yours.
325.practice: List the weeks that sang — by number, by name. Then write one sentence about what they have in common. That's your soul's dialect.

326.title: The Weeks That Resisted
body: And some weeks bounced off. The entries are thin. The practices got skipped. The whole thing felt distant, or dull, or not for you.

Don't skip these in the review — they're the other half of the map. The resistance is information: it tells you where the work is, or where the curriculum's language isn't your language yet, or where life was simply too loud that month.
No guilt. The review isn't a courtroom. "Week 27 didn't land" is a fact, not a failure. Next year, it might. Or the year after. The curriculum is patient; be patient with yourself.
326.practice: Name the weeks that resisted — without explanation or apology. Then add one line: what was happening in your life that week? Sometimes the resistance isn't about the week at all.

327.title: The Ones That Stayed
body: Forty-nine weeks of practices. Which ones are still alive?

Not the ones you admired — the ones you do. The three-breath pause before the blessing. The Friday song. The one-line journal. The midnight minute. The practices that survived the year are the curriculum's real graduates: they made it from the page into the life.
Count them. There are fewer than you think, and they're worth more than you think. Three living practices outweigh thirty admired ones.
327.practice: List the practices you actually still do — honestly. Circle the three most alive. These are your curriculum now.

328.title: The Gaps
body: The weeks you skipped. The days the journal stayed closed. The practices that died by week 30.

Name them — and then let them go. The gaps are part of the year too. A curriculum with no gaps is a curriculum that wasn't lived in a real life. You have a real life; it interrupted. That's not a flaw in the year — that's the year, happening.
The tradition's calendar has gaps too — days without special practices, weeks that are just weeks. The gaps are where the ordinary life breathes. Don't pave them over with guilt.
328.practice: Write the gaps down — one line. Then write, underneath: "The year held them." Close the notebook.

329.title: The Gratitude
body: The review's last word is gratitude. Not for the curriculum — for the year. For the mornings it met you. For the weeks that sang. For the practices that stayed. For the gaps, even.

There's a blessing for completing a study: hadran alach — "we will return to you." Say it to the year. Not goodbye — we'll return. The curriculum is a cycle; the review is the turn of the wheel. You'll walk it again, and it'll be a different year, because you'll be a different walker.
Gratitude is the review's seal. The year, examined, is found — underneath everything — to have been a gift.
329.practice: Write three gratitudes — for the year, specific. Not "I'm grateful for the curriculum" but "I'm grateful for the Tuesday in Cheshvan when..." Specific. True.
329.teaser: making it permanent: from curriculum to life.

330.title: The Transition
body: The curriculum is ending. The life isn't.

This is the delicate week — the transition from studying the year to living it. For forty-eight weeks you've had a guide: a week, a theme, a practice, a teaser. Now the guide steps back. What's left is what you carry.

The question isn't "what did you learn?" It's "what stays when the curriculum goes?" A curriculum you need forever isn't a curriculum — it's a crutch. The real thing stands on its own: in your morning, your week, your year.
330.practice: Write the three practices that stay — from yesterday's review, or fresh. These are no longer "the curriculum's practices." They're yours now. Name them as yours.
330.teaser: the morning: the practice that anchors the day.

331.title: The Morning
body: Everything permanent starts in the morning. The day is the curriculum's first unit (week 1) and its last anchor: however the year goes, the morning returns.

Choose one morning practice — just one — and make it non-negotiable. The blessing on waking. The three breaths. The verse. The journal line. Small enough to keep on the worst day; real enough to matter on the best day.
"Begin with three" was the beginner's rule. The permanent version: keep one. One practice, kept for years, outweighs a hundred practices kept for weeks.
331.practice: Choose the one morning practice. Write it on a card, by the bed. Start tomorrow.
331.teaser: the week: Shabbat as the anchor.

332.title: The Weekly Anchor
body: The week needs an anchor too — and the tradition hands you one: Shabbat. The seventh day, the palace in time, the week complete.
Your permanent weekly practice: whatever Shabbat already is for you, plus one thing the year gave you. The Friday song (week 3's room). The weekly portrait (week 46). The review of the
week's face. One addition, kept.
The curriculum taught you that every week has a face. The permanent version: you keep looking at the face, every week, for the rest of your life. That's not a practice — that's a way of seeing.
332.practice: Choose the one weekly practice — the Shabbat addition. Write it next to the morning card.

333.title: The Monthly Turn
body: And the month: Rosh Chodesh, the new moon, the month's beginning. The tradition's monthly reset — twelve (or thirteen) fresh starts a year.
Your permanent monthly practice: on Rosh Chodesh, one review. The month behind — what lit up, what resisted. The month ahead — one intention. Five minutes. The journal, the moon, the turn.
The curriculum gave you the year's map; Rosh Chodesh gives you the monthly checkpoint. Twelve times a year, you stop and look: where am I in the year? Where is the year in me?
333.practice: Mark the next Rosh Chodesh on your calendar — with one word: "review." Five minutes, monthly, permanent.
333.teaser: the year: the cycle you'll walk again.

334.title: The Again
body: You'll walk the year again. Not the curriculum — the year. The holidays will come, the seasons will turn, the weeks will cycle. And now you'll walk them with eyes the curriculum trained.

That's the permanent version of everything: the second year. The first year you learned the map; the second year you walk the territory. The shofar will sound different. The Omer will count different. Pesach will taste different. Not because the year changed — because you did.
Hadran alach — we will return. The curriculum's last promise is a return ticket.
334.practice: Write one sentence to the you who'll start the next cycle: what to watch for, what to linger on, what to forgive. Seal it. Open it when the year turns.

335.title: The Teaching
body: The permanent version has one more layer: teaching. Not lecturing — sharing. The beginner you were, forty-eight weeks ago, is still out there — in someone you know, or someone you'll meet.

You don't need to teach the curriculum. Teach the one thing: the day holds the year. Or the song. Or the one-line journal. Give away the smallest true thing you found — the way someone once gave it to you (this book, maybe).
The tradition says: teaching fixes the learning in the teacher. What's shared is what's kept.
335.practice: Think of one person. What's the one thing from this year you'd give them? Write it as you'd say it — plain, short, true. You don't have to send it. Yet.

336.title: The Vow
body: End the week with a vow — small, keepable, spoken. Not "I'll do everything" but the three anchors: the morning one, the weekly one, the monthly one.

Say it out loud. A vow spoken is a vow kept differently from a vow thought. The tradition takes vows seriously — which is why this one is small. Small vows get kept; grand vows get admired and abandoned.
"I will [morning practice], every morning. I will [weekly practice], every Shabbat. I will [monthly practice], every Rosh Chodesh." That's the curriculum, permanent: three anchors, held.
336.practice: Speak the vow — out loud, once. Write it under the other cards. Three anchors. Kept.
336.teaser: the sending: the year, carried forward.

337.title: The Return
body: Week 49. Return to week 1.
Read it again — the day that holds the year. The morning that's fall, the afternoon that's spring, the midnight that's the year's turn. Read it with forty-eight weeks behind you.

It's a different week now. The first time, it was a promise: the day holds the year. Now it's a testimony: you've walked the year the day was holding. Every theme week 1 teasered — the songs, the letters, the cycles, the soul — you've lived.
The curriculum is a circle. The end reads the beginning, and the beginning finally makes sense.
337.practice: Reread week 1 — all seven days. Mark the sentence that lands hardest now. That's your year's thesis.
337.teaser: what you carry: the three things.

338.title: The Three Things
body: If you had to carry the whole year in three things — what would they be?
Not three ideas. Three things: three practices, three images, three sentences that are now part of you. The ones you'd pack if the curriculum burned and you could save three pages.
Choose them. Write them on one card — the card you'll keep when the notebook is shelved. The year, distilled: three things.
(If you can't choose three, choose one. One true thing, carried for life, is the whole curriculum succeeded.)
338.practice: The card. Three things — or one. Write it. Keep it where you'll see it.
338.teaser: the blessing: the year behind, blessed.

339.title: Blessing the Behind
body: Bless the year behind. Not the curriculum — the year. The actual days: the mornings, the falls, the songs, the gaps.

The blessing doesn't require the year to have been good. It requires it to have been lived. "Blessed is the year that taught me..." — fill it in, true. Even the hard weeks get blessed: they were part of the walking.
There's a tradition of blessing the past — shehecheyanu looks backward as much as forward. The year behind, blessed, becomes foundation instead of weight.
339.practice: Speak the blessing — out loud, once: "Blessed is the year that..." Fill it true.

340.title: Blessing the Ahead
body: And bless the year ahead — the one you'll walk without the curriculum's hand.

You don't know what it holds. That's the point of the blessing: it doesn't predict, it entrusts. The year ahead, blessed in advance, is met differently — not as a threat, as a territory. You've walked one year with a map; now you walk with the map inside you.
The blessing for the ahead is shorter than the blessing for the behind. The behind is known; the ahead is trust.
340.practice: One sentence, spoken: "Blessed is the year ahead — may I walk it..." Fill it, speak it, trust it.
340.teaser: the circle: the end is the beginning.

341.title: The Circle
body: The curriculum's shape is a circle: 49 weeks, seven sevens, complete — and the end touches the beginning.

Week 49's last teaching is the circle itself: nothing here was linear. You didn't climb from ignorance to knowledge; you walked around — the day, the songs, the letters, the cycles — and arrived back where you started, seeing it for the first time.
There's a reason the Torah ends and begins again on the same day. The circle isn't repetition — it's return. The second time around, you're not the same walker. The path isn't the same path.
341.practice: Stand at the year's circle — journal closed, cards kept, vow spoken. Say hadran alach: we will return. Mean it.

342.title: Your Song
body: Week 3 gave you seven songs — the tradition's songs, for the seven days. Now: yours.

Not a composition — a recognition. By now there's a verse, a line, a niggun, a psalm that became yours this year — the one you hummed without deciding to, the one that surfaced in the hard week. That's your song. Every walker gets one by the end.
The tradition's songs were the curriculum. Your song is the graduation: the soul, singing — not the curriculum's song anymore, but its own, in the curriculum's key.
342.practice: Name your song — the verse, the line, the tune. Sing it, say it, write it on the card with the three things. Yours.
342.teaser: the door: the last day of the forty-nine.

343.title: The Door
body: Day 343. The last day of the forty-nine. (Seven sevens, complete — like the Omer's count, like the jubilee's eve.)
Before you: a door. Behind it, the Mochin — the three weeks of Chochmah, Binah, Da'at, hovering over the year's midnight seam. The curriculum's crown, and the year's turn.

But today: the door itself. Stand in it a moment. Look back at the forty-nine weeks — the day, the songs, the letters, the cycles, the worlds, the soul, the living of it. Look ahead at the three that remain — the mind's crown, the year's midnight.
Then step through. The journal is closed; the cards are kept; the vow is spoken; the song is yours. What's left is the highest thing — and the year's turn.
The Mochin (weeks 50–52)

Above the year's midnight — the Chatzot seam, where the year turns — hover three weeks: the Mochin, the mind's crown. Chochmah, Binah, Da'at. The curriculum's last ascent: fifteen steps, climbed in the small hours, before the year begins again.
First: Chochmah. Wisdom — not as knowledge, as flash.
343.practice: Write the last journal line of the forty-nine: one sentence, the whole year. Then close the notebook. Step through.

344.title: The Lightning
body: Chochmah is lightning. It doesn't arrive by argument; it strikes — a flash, whole, all at once. You've known this: the insight that lands complete before you can explain it. The solution that appears before the reasoning. The verse that opens before the commentary.

The tradition calls Chochmah the beginning — not the first step, the flash before the steps. Every week of this year began as a flash in someone's mind before it became a curriculum. Every practice you kept began as a strike.
344.practice: Catch one flash today — the insight that arrives whole. Don't explain it yet. Just notice: lightning.
344.teaser: the seed: the whole tree, in miniature.

345.title: The Seed
body: A seed holds the tree — not as a description, as a reality. Chochmah is the seed-mind: the whole thing, compressed, potential, waiting.

Week 1 was a seed: "the day holds the year" — seven days that held forty-nine weeks. You couldn't see the tree then. Now you can. But the tree was in the seed from the start; the year didn't add it, it unfolded it.
That's Chochmah's lesson about everything: the whole is in the beginning. The end doesn't complete the start — it reveals it.
345.practice: Hold one seed-thought from this year — the first flash you remember. See the tree it became. The seed, honored.

346.title: The Beginning
body: "Reishit chochmah — the beginning of wisdom is awe." The tradition's first sentence about wisdom: it begins not with brilliance, with awe.

Awe is the mind's honesty: before the vastness, the flash admits its size. Chochmah's lightning doesn't make you greater; it shows you the sky. The bigger the flash, the bigger the awe — because the flash reveals how much more there is.
Fifty weeks in, the awe should be larger than at the start. If it is, the curriculum worked.
346.practice: Stand before one vast thing today — the sky, the sea, the year's circle — and let the mind go quiet. Awe: the beginning.

347.title: The Not-Knowing
body: Chochmah's secret: it's the wisdom of not-knowing. The flash illuminates — and what it illuminates, first, is the darkness around it.

The tradition says Chochmah is ayin — nothingness. Not emptiness: the fertile nothing before the something. The mind at its highest doesn't grasp; it opens. "I don't know" — said truly, at the right moment — is Chochmah speaking.
After forty-nine weeks of learning, the crown is unlearning: holding the whole curriculum lightly, knowing it's a finger pointing, not the moon.
347.practice: Say "I don't know" once today — about something that matters — and mean it as wisdom, not defeat. The fertile nothing.

348.title: The Thirty-Two Paths
body: The tradition counts thirty-two paths of wisdom — the channels the flash travels: ten sefirot and twenty-two letters. Chochmah doesn't strike at random; it runs along paths.

You've walked these paths all year without naming them: the ten cycles (the sefirot-paths), the alphabet weeks (the letter-paths). Every flash you caught traveled a path the curriculum laid. The lightning needs the rods.
That's why the Mochin come last: the paths had to be built before the crown could descend. Fifty weeks of paths; now the flash that walks them.
348.practice: Trace one flash back along its path — which week laid the road it traveled? The lightning, grounded.

349.title: The Father
body: Chochmah is called the father — Abba. Not as authority; as source. The father gives the seed; the mother (Binah — next week) builds the child.

The year's father-seed was week 1's flash: the day holds the year. Everything since was gestation. Fifty weeks of building the child — and now, at the crown, you meet the father again: the seed, recognized.

Every beginning you've ever lived had this structure: a flash (father), a building (mother), a birth (the thing itself). Learn to spot the father-moments — they're the ones that feel like lightning and turn out to be seeds.
349.practice: Name one father-moment in your life — a flash that became a building. Honor the seed.
349.teaser: catching the flash: the week's close.

350.title: Caught
body: The week's close: catch the flash. Chochmah strikes and vanishes — unless it's caught. The catching is Binah's work (next week), but the readiness is this week's practice: the mind, open, attentive, quick.

The tradition's image: the mind like a vessel, polished, waiting. The flash comes to the ready mind — not the fullest mind, the readiest. Fifty weeks of curriculum: that's the polishing. The vessel, prepared.
Tonight, at the year's midnight hour if you can: sit in the readiness. The flash may come. Or not. The readiness is the practice.
The Mochin (weeks 50–52)
The flash struck. Now: the building. Binah — understanding — is the palace the lightning builds. Chochmah is the seed; Binah is the gestation. The father gave the flash; the mother builds the child.
350.practice: Five minutes of readiness — mind open, vessel polished, waiting. The flash, welcomed.
350.teaser: Binah: the palace. The flash, built.

351.title: The Building
body: Binah builds. The flash arrives whole but unusable — a seed can't be eaten. Understanding is the slow work: turning the lightning into architecture, the seed into a tree you can live in.

You've done this all year: every flash the curriculum struck, you built — practices, journal lines, the three things on the card. The building is less glamorous than the lightning and more important. Unbuilt flashes fade; built ones become palaces.
351.practice: Take one flash from last week — one Chochmah-strike — and build one room: one practice, one sentence, one action. The palace, begun.

352.title: The Fifty Gates
body: The tradition counts fifty gates of understanding — the palace's rooms. Forty-nine are given; the fiftieth is the mystery (the jubilee's gate, the one beyond reach).

Fifty-one weeks. You've passed through forty-nine gates — the forty-nine weeks of the curriculum's body. This week is the fiftieth gate's threshold: the understanding that the palace is bigger than any room you've entered.
The fifty gates teach: understanding is endless. Every room opens onto another. The palace doesn't complete — it deepens. That's not a flaw; it's the design. Binah's joy is the next room.
352.practice: Stand at the threshold — name the forty-nine rooms (the weeks) in one breath, then rest at the fiftieth: the room beyond. Understanding, endless.

353.title: The Mother
body: Binah is called the mother — Imma. The father (Chochmah) gives the seed in a flash; the mother carries it, builds it, births it — slowly, in the dark, over time.

Fifty-one weeks: that's a gestation. The curriculum was a pregnancy — the seed of week 1, carried through the songs, the letters, the cycles, the soul, the living — until now, at the crown, the birth is near.

Honor the slowness. The tradition's mothers don't hurry. Understanding can't be rushed; the child comes when it comes. Your impatience with the slow weeks was the father's impatience. The mother's answer: gestation.
353.practice: Thank one slow thing in your life — the understanding that took years, the practice that took months. The mother's pace, honored.

354.title: The Contemplation
body: Binah's practice is contemplation — hitbonenut: taking one thing and turning it, and turning it, until it opens. Not studying — dwelling. The flash is quick; the dwelling is slow.

Take one verse. One line from the year. One of your three things. Turn it: what does it mean? What else? What's underneath? What's it asking of me? The turning is the practice; the opening is the gift.
The tradition says the heart understands — lev meivin. Contemplation isn't head-work; it's heart- work. The thing, turned in the heart, until the heart knows it.
354.practice: Fifteen minutes of contemplation — one line, turned and turned. The dwelling.

355.title: The Heart Understands
body: "Lev meivin — the heart understands." The tradition locates Binah not in the head but in the heart. Understanding, at its depth, is cardiac.

You've felt this: the moment a teaching drops from the head to the heart — from "I see" to "I know." The curriculum aimed at this drop all year. The head learns the map; the heart walks the territory. Fifty-one weeks: the long fall from head to heart.
Binah's palace has its foundation in the chest. The flash struck the mind; the building settles in the heart. When the heart understands, the practice keeps itself.
355.practice: Feel for the drop — one teaching that's fallen from head to heart this year. Name it. The heart, understanding.

356.title: Flash Into Structure
body: Watch the pair work: Chochmah flashes, Binah structures. The year's own example — week 1 flashed "the day holds the year"; forty-nine weeks structured it into curriculum. The lightning; the rods.

This is how everything real gets made: the strike, then the building. Skip the strike, and the building is hollow. Skip the building, and the strike is wasted. The Mochin's first two weeks are the complete creative act — and now you know its anatomy.
Your life's works: check them against the pair. Which had lightning but no building? Which had building but no lightning? The pair, complete, is the only thing that stands.
356.practice: Take one unfinished thing in your life — diagnose it: missing the flash, or missing the building? Supply what's missing.

357.title: Transformed
body: Binah's last secret: understanding transforms. Not informs — transforms. The palace you build around the flash becomes the house you live in; the house changes the dweller.
You're not the person who started week 1. The understanding didn't just add rooms to your mind — it rebuilt the dweller. Fifty-one weeks of building: the builder, rebuilt.
The tradition's word for this is da'at — but that's next week. This week's close is the recognition: the palace worked. You're inside it. It's inside you.
The Mochin (weeks 50–52)
The last week. Da'at — knowledge — the key that joins the flash and the palace, the crown that gathers the year. Above the Chatzot seam, at the year's midnight: the turn.
357.practice: Look at the dweller — the you in the palace. What's different? Write the transformation in one sentence. The building, complete.
357.teaser: Da'at: the key. The year's last week.

358.title: The Key
body: Da'at is the key — the tradition's image. Chochmah and Binah are the two chambers; Da'at is the key that opens between them, the connector. Knowledge, here, isn't information — it's joining.

You've known Da'at all year without naming it: every time a flash became a practice, every time an understanding became a doing — that joining was Da'at. The key, turning, all year. This week names the turner.
The Mochin's anatomy, complete: the flash (Chochmah), the palace (Binah), the key (Da'at). Strike, build, join. Nothing real lacks the third.
358.practice: Turn the key once today — join one understanding to one action. The flash, the palace, the joining.

359.title: The Bridge
body: Da'at is the bridge between the mind's two banks: Chochmah's lightning on one side, Binah's architecture on the other. Without the bridge, the flash can't reach the palace; the palace can't receive the flash.

The year's bridge: every practice was a plank. The journal (week 46) bridged the weeks to the witness. The vow (week 48) bridged the curriculum to the life. The song (week 49) bridged the tradition to the soul.
Check your bridges. The flashes that never became buildings are missing Da'at. The buildings with no lightning are missing it too. The key, the bridge: the third thing that makes the pair one.
359.practice: Find one unbridged pair in your life — a flash without a building, or a building without a flash — and lay one plank. The bridge, built.

360.title: And Adam Knew
body: The Torah's word for the deepest joining is knowing: "and Adam knew Eve." Da'at is intimate knowledge — the knower and the known, joined.

This is the week's depth: Da'at isn't about the year, it's with the year. You've spent fifty-two weeks not studying time but knowing it — intimately, the way you know a person. The year's face, its moods, its songs: known.
The curriculum's last intimacy: the year isn't an object anymore. It's a relationship. And relationships are known by Da'at — by joining, not by studying.
360.practice: Know the year the way you know a person — write it a letter. "Dear year..." The intimacy, spoken.
360.teaser: the gathering: all fifty-two, in one point.

361.title: The Gathering
body: Da'at gathers. Fifty-two weeks — the day, the songs, the letters, the cycles, the worlds, the soul, the living, the flash, the palace — gather into a single point of knowing.

Not a summary: a singularity. The way a life gathers at a deathbed, or a year at midnight. All of it, present, at once. The curriculum's fifty-two rooms collapse into one chamber — and the chamber is you.
Sit in the gathering. Don't sort it, don't review it — hold it. All fifty-two weeks, held, in one point, in one heart. That's Da'at: the all, known as one.
361.practice: Ten minutes of gathering — the year, held whole, in one point. No sorting. Holding.

362.title: The Seam
body: The Chatzot seam: the year's midnight. Above it hovered these three weeks — the Mochin, the eighty-eight minutes, the fifteen steps. Now the seam itself.

At midnight, the day turns. At the year's midnight, the year turns. Behind: the fifty-two weeks you walked. Ahead: Tishrei, the beginning, the year again. The seam is the hinge — the moment that belongs to neither year and makes both possible.
The tradition's midnight practices live here: the lament, the study, the fifteen ascents. You've been climbing them for three weeks. Tonight: the top of the steps. The hinge. The turn.
362.practice: At midnight — or the midnight you can keep — mark the seam. A minute of silence at the hinge. The year, turning.

363.title: The Restart
body: Tishrei. The year's beginning — one of its two beginnings (the fall's Rosh Hashanah; the spring's Nissan). The curriculum ends where the year begins: at the restart.

But it's not the same Tishrei. Last Tishrei, you hadn't walked the year. This Tishrei, you have. The shofar will sound — and you'll hear fifty-two weeks in it. The prayers will come — and you'll pray them with the year's body behind you.
Hadran alach: we will return — and here is the return. The restart isn't the curriculum's end; it's the year's beginning. The curriculum was the preparation. The year is the thing.
363.practice: Greet the restart — one blessing for the new year, spoken with the old year's voice. The beginning, again, for the first time.
363.teaser: the last day: a year inside the day.

364.title: The Day
body: Day 364. The last day. And the title: A Year Inside the Day.

Week 1 promised it: the day holds the year. Fifty-two weeks proved it: the songs, the letters, the cycles, the worlds, the soul, the living, the mind's crown — all of it, inside the day's hours. Morning (fall), midday (winter), afternoon (spring), night (summer), midnight (the turn).

So: live one day — today — as the whole year. Morning: begin (Tishrei). Midday: learn (the winter's depth). Afternoon: free (Nissan's exodus). Evening: gather (the summer's fullness). Night: turn (the seam). One day, the year entire.
The curriculum is complete. The day remains. And the day — as week 1 said, as day 364 proves — holds everything.
A year inside the day. The day inside you.
364.practice: Live today as the year — the five seasons of the day, walked deliberately. The title, fulfilled.
364.teaser: Hadran alach — we will return. Begin again.
